newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle astronauts light fires in space.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle astronauts light fires in space.

text.p: Astronauts aboard the U.S. space shuttle Columbia set up their orbiting laboratory on Wednesday and began a $86 million scientific research programme, NASA officials said.

Astronaut Janice Voss lit the first of 144 controlled fires inside a special compartment in the shuttle's bus-sized laboratory module shortly before 4 p.m. EDT (2000 GMT), NASA's mission commentator Anthony Jacob said.
One of the major goals of the 33 scientific experiments planned for Columbia's 16-day flight was to study the behaviour of fire in space.
Scientists hoped the combustion research could lead to improvements in fuel efficiency in cars, jet engines and heating appliances.
Other experiments packed aboard the shuttle's European-built Spacelab will attempt to grow protein crystals to aid medical research and manufacture new alloys.

It was a second chance for astronauts to accomplish their research. Their first attempt at the mission in April was cut short after only five days aloft because of a troublesome electricity generator aboard Columbia.
"It's good to be back," Voss told mission control as she floated into the laboratory after the shuttle's blastoff from Florida's Kennedy Space Centre on Tuesday afternoon.
NASA prepared Columbia for another attempt at the mission in near-record time. It was the first time an entire shuttle crew had returned to space to complete unfinished business.

"The science teams are indeed very excited to be flying again," mission scientist Michael Robinson told a news conference. "From the first flight they know their experiments were working. It's just time now to bring them to a definitive conclusion."

The shuttle crew caught a brief glimpse of the stricken Russian Mir space station on Wednesday morning. The two craft passed at high speed, about 60 miles (100 km) apart and in entirely different orbits.
Although a docking on this mission is not possible, NASA was trying to see if the two space crews could chat by radio, mission operations director Jeff Bantle said.
Columbia and its seven astronauts were due back to Earth on July 17.
